# Examining Exposure Differences between Residential and Smartphone Mobility-Based Greenness in a Cohort of the Nurses’ Health Study

**Authors:** Grete E. Wilt; Charlotte Roscoe; Cindy R. Hu; Hari S. Iyer; Unnati V. Mehta; Brent A. Coull; Jaime E. Hart; Steven Gortmaker; Francine Laden; Peter James

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Environmental Health, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 2Channing Division of Network Medicine, Department of Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 3Division of Population Sciences, Dana Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 4Department of Biostatistics, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 5Department of Social and Behavioral Sciences, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 6Department of Population Medicine, Harvard Medical School and Harvard Pilgrim Health Care Institute, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## Introduction

In epidemiological studies, greenness exposure is often measured by calculating the mean satellite-derived Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) within circular buffers around residential addresses.1,2 These buffers can range from $100 meters$ to $greater than 1000 plus meters$ radius to represent the environment directly surrounding one’s residence or accessible within walking distance.3 Buffers may fail to accurately capture personal greenness exposure at locations outside of the residential buffer.1,2,4 The discrepancy between measured exposures and true spatial and temporal boundaries of the exposure exerting contextual influences, like greenness, is known as the uncertain geographic context problem.5,6 Spatial delineation of an exposure, rather than the exposure itself, may influence the association observed. Thus, commonly used greenness exposures may not provide an accurate reflection of the true exposure for each individual, potentially biasing epidemiological results.2,5,6 We compared greenness exposure quantified with traditional residential buffers and novel mobility-based estimates from smartphone global positioning systems (GPS).

## Methods

The nationally representative Nurses’ Health Study 3 Mobile Health Substudy7 tracked 337 participants living in 42 out of 50 states across the United States for four 7-d sampling periods across a year, using a customized smartphone application (developed by Overlap Health, Inc.) from 2018 to 2020. Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Pilgrim Health Care Institute (Boston, Massachusetts) provided institutional review board approval. Upon meeting eligibility requirements, participants consented through an electronic form. Landsat-derived NDVI ( $30 meters$ resolution) was used to calculate residential (annual and seasonal average $270 meter$ and $1230 meter$ circular buffers; Figure 1A) and mobility-based greenness. We used these two residential measures of greenness because $270 meter$ residential buffers represent visible distance and $1230 meter$ residential buffers represent walkable distance buffers in the literature.3 We calculated mobility-based greenness exposure using seasonally matched NDVI values for GPS points captured every 10 min. Three mobility-based NDVI metrics were developed (Figure 1B–D): all mobility, nonwork mobility (GPS points using a $100 meter$ buffer to exclude work locations), and active transportation mobility [defined as GPS mobility data points with velocities that fell between walking and running (0.8– $0.8 to 4 meters per second$ )8]. Time stamps in addition to GPS locations were used to estimate velocity and restricted analyses to velocities that fell between walking and running (0.8– $0.8 to 4 meters per second$ ) to obtain data points of active transport or recreating. We chose this approach because we hypothesized that participants might be more likely to engage in active transport in green spaces. Nonactive transport exposures are captured in the all mobility and nonwork mobility models. We calculated descriptive statistics and used Bland-Altman plots to assess agreement between the residential and mobility-derived greenness exposures.9

*Figure 1.: Four panel exposure map comparison of (A) residential buffers, (B) all GPS mobility data, (C) nonwork GPS mobility data (GPS points using a $100 meter$ buffer to exclude work locations), and (D) active transport [GPS mobility data points with velocities that fell between walking and running (0.8 to $0.8 to 4 meters per second$ )]. Data for (A)–(D) are generated from author’s Strava data for descriptive purposes only and do not reflect an actual participant’s data. Stationary data points have a velocity of $0 meter per second$ up to $0.8 meter per second$ , active transport data points fell between 0.8 to $0.8 to 4 meters per second$ , and automated transport was classified as data points above $4 meters per second$ . Figure 1A–1D were produced in ArcGIS Pro. Note: GPS, Global Positioning System.*

We also performed Bland-Altman tests stratified by season, walkability, and neighborhood socioeconomic status (nSES). We defined neighborhood walkability as a composite score of intersection density calculated from 2019 Tiger/Line shapefiles of all roads with interstates removed (www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files/time-series/geo/tiger-line-file.html), population density from 2019 American Community Survey population data, and 2018 business density data from Infogroup US Historical Business Data (https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/PNOFKI). Variables were z-standardized at the tract for the entire 2010 U.S. Census and summed to create a neighborhood walkability index. Higher scores indicate more walkable areas. We joined these data based on date and location of each GPS point for an aggregated measure of a mobility-based value of neighborhood walkability. We categorized values into high and low walkability, on the mean.

We measured nSES using a composite score of seven Census tract–level variables representing domains that have been previously associated with health outcomes, including education, employment, housing, wealth, racial composition, and population density.10 Variables were carried forward from the prior U.S. Census (2010), and each variable was z-standardized and summed to create a nSES score. Higher scores indicated higher nSES. We joined quartiles of nSES score using the location of each GPS point to create a mobility-based nSES score. We categorized values into high and low nSES, on the mean.

All analyses were completed using R (version 4.2; R Development Core Team).

## Results

Descriptive statistics illustrated that this population comprised predominantly White, educated women with a mean age of 36 y (Table 1). Mean annual NDVI values from residential-based buffers [ $270 meters equals 0.40$ , standard deviation (SD) 0.12; $1230 meters equals 0.39$ (SD 0.12)] were higher than from mobility-based NDVI ( $mean equals 0.32$ , $standard deviation equals 0.11$ ). Mean annual NDVI values were lowest for active transportation-only mobility (0.28, $standard deviation equals 0.09$ ). The Bland-Altman agreement bias was 7.8% [95% confidence interval (CI): 6.7%, 8.9%] and 7.3% (95% CI: 6.3%, 8.4%) for $270 meters$ and $1230 meters$ residential NDVI, respectively, in comparison with mobility-based NDVI. There was no evidence of bias between the two residential-based buffer measures (0.5%, 95% CI: $negative 0.1 percent$ , 1.0%). We observed similar trends in these analyses with nonwork and active transportation mobility data; however, the strongest trends were observed in the full data set. In analyses stratified by season, agreement bias between residential and mobility-based measures was lower in winter ( $270 meters$ : 4.3%, 95% CI: 3.1%, 5.6%) and higher in summer ( $270 meters$ : 12.0%, 95% CI: 10.5%, 13.4%). Agreement bias differed when stratified by walkability. In low walkability neighborhoods, the agreement bias with the mobility-based NDVI was 9.0% (95% CI: 7.7, 10.3) for the $270 meter$ NDVI and 8.3% (95% CI: 7.0, 9.7) for the $1230 meter$ NDVI. In high walkability neighborhoods, agreement bias for residential-based and mobility-based NDVI was 5.1% (95% CI: 3.0, 7.2) ( $270 meters$ ) and 5.2% (95% CI: 3.1, 7.2) ( $1230 meters$ ). In Bland-Altman analyses stratified by nSES, there were no statistically significant differences across strata [ $270 meter$ NDVI: low nSES: 8.4% (95% CI: 6.8, 9.9); high nSES: 7.5% (95% CI: 5.9, 9.2); and $1230 meter$ NDVI: low nSES: 7.2% (95% CI: 5.5, 8.8); high nSES: 7.6% (95% CI: 6.1, 9.1)].

## Discussion

In this analysis comparing residential-based to smartphone GPS–based exposure to greenness, residential-based estimates were higher than mobility-based estimates. We did not observe a difference when comparing the two residential distance measures to each other. Our findings support the phenomenon known as neighborhood effect averaging, which suggests erroneous results are produced from reliance on residential exposure estimates. Assuming mobility-based exposure represents personal exposure, this finding suggests the presence of nondifferential measurement error in residential measures of greenness. The error is likely nondifferential because exposure is independent of outcome status. This error was the lowest in winter and in low walkability neighborhoods. No differences in measurement error were observed when stratifying on nSES. As such, although it is important to consider that, on average, GPS mobility-based greenness exposure may be lower than residential exposure for individuals in low walkability areas and in warmer months, measurement error does not change with respect to an individual’s nSES.

Our findings contribute to discussions on the optimal spatial scale of exposures and grappling with the uncertain geographic context problem.6 Although varying-sized residential buffers produced similar exposure estimates, mobility-based greenness estimates were lower on average than residential buffers. Ideally, future analyses should use smartphone GPS data as gold-standard exposures in measurement error correction models.
